# Converging Measures and an Emergent Model: A Meta-Analysis of Human-Machine Trust Questionnaires

[YOSEF S. RAZIN](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1630-8929) and [KAREN M. FEIGH](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0281-7634), School of Aerospace Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia, USA

Trust is crucial for technological acceptance, continued usage, and teamwork. However, human-robot trust, and human-machine trust more generally, suffer from terminological disagreement and construct proliferation. By comparing, mapping, and analyzing well-constructed trust survey instruments, this work uncovers a consensus structure of trust in human–machine interaction. To do so, we identify the most frequently cited and best-validated human-machine and human-robot trust questionnaires as well as the best-established factors that form the dimensions and antecedents of such trust. To reduce both confusion and construct proliferation, we provide a detailed mapping of terminology between questionnaires. Furthermore, we perform a meta-analysis of the regression models which emerged from the experiments that employed multi-factorial survey instruments. Based on this meta-analysis, we provide the most complete, experimentally validated model of human-machine and human-robot trust to date. This convergent model establishes an integrated framework for future research. It determines the current boundaries of trust measurement and where further investigation and validation are necessary. We close by discussing how to choose an appropriate trust survey instrument and how to design for trust. By identifying the internal workings of trust, a more complete basis for measuring trust is developed that is widely applicable.

CCS Concepts: • Human-centered computing → HCI theory, concepts and models; User models; • General and reference → Surveys and overviews; Design; • Computing methodologies → Modeling methodologies;

Additional Key Words and Phrases: Human-Robot Trust, Shared Mental Models

## 1 Introduction

Though still fractured into multiple sub-fields and suffering from construct proliferation, after three decades of sustained research, a complete model is finally emerging for human-robot and human-automation trust. The past few years have proven particularly fruitful, yielding many models, measurement instruments, and meta-reviews. However, much research in these areas is heavily siloed, such that established researchers tend to use assessments that are familiar, and new researchers seeking a trust assessment are often at a loss, trying to make sense of the various models and distinct terminology used by each sub-field and even specific research groups. The greatest challenge they face is which survey instrument to use to measure trust and how to assess its validity. This gap in standards has led many to create their own instruments, making cross comparisons difficult.

In response, numerous attempts have been made to bring order to chaos. Most notably, McKnight and Chervany [101] performed a meta-review to create a trust typology for e-commerce, which later developed into their work on trust in specific technology [99]. Lee and See [78] produced a seminal review of trust in automation, sorting and categorizing trust definitions and their keywords, and presented an integrated model of trust calibration over time. Gefen et al. [43] presented an extensive mapping of trust conceptualizations in e-commerce, and then proceeded to validate an integrative model experimentally. Further systematic reviews of trust in automation models and findings were performed by Hoff and Bashir [60] and Hancock et al. [50], the latter including a meta-analysis of results, which was recently updated [51]. A general review of trust measurement was presented by French et al. [41] and a small qualitative meta-analysis of trust survey instruments has also been presented [13]. Beyond these critical works were also dozens of papers and dissertations which have made varying contributions (e.g., [29, 59, 61, 134, 138, 181]).

While each of these works made significant contributions, it is clear that much work remains. Many assessments still focus on fulfilling niche requirements, and there is limited cross-communication between sub-fields. Results are often mixed, and the way forward remains unaddressed. Progress has been most concrete in the development of survey instruments [43, 99, 138], but empirical validation is spotty, and construct proliferation has stifled progress.

This paper proposes a way forward, leveraging the reliability and validation analysis of the existing survey instruments, to demonstrate the current convergent, established state of the overall field thus far. We take a similar approach to that performed for human-human trust by McEvily and Tortoriello [97] and utilize a meta-analysis. The meta-analysis will (1) identify the most cited survey instruments and examine their validity and reliability, (2) identify the best-validated instruments, (3) identify trust-related factors within survey instruments that have shown reliability and validity and provide a comprehensive mapping of terminology between these factors, (4) establish the internal model from which trust is composed and how the various factors influence one another from the meta-analysis data, (5) provide guidance on choosing and designing future assessments of trust and, finally, (6) outline what the next steps are in validating the overall model and where we go from here.

Many trust papers at this point review the multitude of trust definitions [43, 100, 112, 138]. As this paper aims to identify the converging validated concept beneath human-machine trust from the current survey instruments, we leave our definition<sup>1</sup>as open as possible.

Trust is a state effectuated by the trustor in which the trustee has power over some subset of the trustor’s goals that the trustor believes they could not accomplish with a better net outcome on their own.

The state may be an attitude [78, 106], belief [43], expectation [112], judgement [78, 106], willingness [45, 73, 89, 100], confidence [45, 89], or reliance [50]. The perceived power of the trustee over the trustor’s goals is often expressed in terms of the trustor’s vulnerability, uncertainty, or risk [138]. In this work, we will be focused on the trustee as some sort of specific technological system, such as a robot or AI-driven machines. As our stated goal herein is to identify a single structure emerging from the various sub-fields, we leave the discussion of how trust may differ between types of technology until the end.

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>1</sup>most closely related to those of [15, 78, 84, 136, 184]</span></small>

Here we take a bottom-up approach to demonstrate what factors and interactions influence trust and its correlates and how to measure them. Only then will we attempt to extract what parts are trusted directly instead of antecedents or correlates. When needed for clarity, we will note when factor names differ from standard definitions or are used in non-standard ways.

## 2 Background

Thus, this work aims to cover the cognitive structure underlying trust. By cognitive, we do not mean capability-based trust but trust as it is explicitly and consciously conceived of by participants and, therefore, amenable to self-report. Thus, for example, we are not looking at the appearance of the robot per se but the human’s perception of the robot, e.g., that it appears friendly or that they are comfortable around it. Design, appearance, and other external factors certainly shape trust, but we focus only on identifiable internal cognitive factors that compose trust. This focus on internal, cognitive trust establishes a stronger foundation for understanding how and why external factors affect trust.

Given our focus on internal factors, one might ask about what differentiates trust in humans vs. technological systems, manual vs. interactive vs. fully autonomous systems, “dumb” vs. smart AIs, and systems that are more embodied, e.g., robots vs. ones that are only interacted with via a single limited interface, e.g., computers. Each difference between these realizations could be significant in how trust is perceived. One such debate exists around the computer-as-social actor (CASA) theory of Nass et al. [114, 115]. This theory posits that technological systems, including autonomy [88] and robots [33, 116], are treated fundamentally as human “social actors,” including with regard to reciprocity [79] and trust [88]. It is important to distinguish if trust is thought of the same way between humans and machines instead of whether different types of agents elicit different response levels (i.e., structure vs. content). Many studies have indeed shown that humans may trust non-human agents more or less than humans [28, 88, 105] perhaps having different trust thresholds. However, as we will demonstrate below (Section 8.3), humans do seem to frame trust with the same factors and antecedents for machines that they use for humans. Thus, our focus here is on multi-factorial, multi-dimensional internal human-machine trust models. The term “machine” in this context includes robots, artificial intelligence (AI), computers, and technological systems.

The largest initial attempt to synthesize a similar interdisciplinary conception of trust was produced by McKnight and Chervany [101]. Their meta-analysis on definitions of trust and its components covered 60 publications in four fields—management, sociology, political science, and psychology during the last third of the 20th century. While they proposed some tentative models, the major contribution of this work was to capture a glimpse of the confusion over the terminology and the disparate definitions historically attributed to trust. They especially shed light on two major disputes over trust—how its conceived (personal vs impersonal, affective vs cognitive, belief vs intent) and the type and number of attributes it encompasses (competence, predictability, benevolence, etc.). They also propose a layered black-box model of trust, that while lacking in internal dynamics or analysis, outlined a generalized structure by which to decompose trust.

Major reviews by Hancock et al. [50, 51], Schaefer [138]), and Hoff and Bashir [60] each elucidated key aspects of an integrated trust model, while leaving major gaps in the theory. Hancock et al.’s [50] meta-analysis of trust in human–robot interaction (HRI) looked at 29 papers from the past 25 years and took a different tack. They attempted a qualitative statistical analysis of correlational data between trust attributes while outlining factors that affect trust. These factors were divided into broad categories based on the locus (human, robot, and environment), as well as by agent properties (ability, performance, attributes). Here both the task and team dynamics are analyzed within the work environment. While they found robot-based factors as most impactful, the study was severely limited by the lack of correlational studies that look at human-related ability factors, task-related factors (complexity, multi-tasking, etc.), and issues at the interface such as false alarms and transparency. Schaefer [138] continued with Hancock and others on this previous work to refine the factors they identified in the broader context of human–automation interaction (HAI), though in this meta-analysis their factors only accounted for half of the effect size on overall trust development. This work further divided the human- and robot-related analyses to account for emotive, error, and feedback factors—most importantly highlighting that emotive factors have some of the highest correlational effects on trust. A third major update by Hancock et al. [51], expanded their meta-analysis to 45 articles, found support for many of the factors they had previously proposed as being important but at the time had been untested such as user comfort, culture, expertise, and personality. This review posited six major categories of factors that affect trust: Characteristic-based, Ability-Based, Attribute-Based, Performance-Based, Tasking, and Team collaboration. The major goal of this series of analyses was to fully cover every possible factor that may affect trust.

A more structurally-focused tack was taken in the major literature review by Hoff and Bashir [60], who attempted an empirical validation of Lee and See [78] by examining 127 studies. They settled on a three-layered model of trust (dispositional, situational, and learned) and five recommendations for future design guidelines for trust. These focused specifically on the interface (anthropomorphism, ease of use, communication style) and feedback (understandability, timing, transparency, and its relationship with the level of automation). Their three-layered model closely paralleled previous works by Muir [112] and McKnight and Chervany [101], though they directly drew it from Marsh and Dibben’s catch-all chapter on trust from information science [92].

A third major literature review [88] specifically focused on understanding human-automation trust as compared to human-human trust. It presented a clearer division of perceptual antecedents and elements of trust from the external factors that influence them. Within their category of cognitive processes relating to trust, they locate Expectations of the Trustee and Perceived Reliability of the Trustee in opposition to Perceptions of Relative Self-Competence, Self-Serving Bias, and Perceived Reliability of Manual Control in a dualistic scheme expanding on a classic two-item trust questionnaire [77].

Beyond these reviews and meta-analyses, models of trust abound [18, 43, 45, 73, 78, 89, 104]. The seeming disparity between these structures is compounded by the variegated and eclectic terms proposed for all the different factors involved. The challenge of making headway is further amplified by researchers’ propensity to throw up their hands in the face of so much complexity and make up their own survey instruments, as we will illustrate.

Thus, while we do not intend to cover the full range of factors that affect trust in robotics and automation, we do aim to derive a more fully explicated structural model of trust in the spirit of Hoff and Bashir [60]. Like them as well, we also chose to limit our scope to internal factors, or psychological constructs within the trustor’s mind relating to trust and its antecedents as opposed to external factors, such as age, gender, anthropomorphism/robot form, display transparency, etc. This is in part because of the ubiquity of subjective measures of trust. However, more importantly, we believe that trust cannot be properly understood without a more phenomenological, cognitive approach. The way trust is processed and trust-related factors are perceived matters in complex ways, that are only now beginning to be appreciated [51]. Once a common foundation of internal trust can be firmly established, a much larger conversation about external characteristics and how they affect the various internal factors can be had much more fruitfully.

Thus, this work is distinct from previous meta-analyses as it does not only list a set of previous trust measures or models and identify common trends among them. We go beyond that by presenting a more detailed analysis of critical works at the factor level. We identify more trust measures than any previous work and assess their reliability and validity at an unprecedented level. We also contribute a new careful mapping of the factor terminology between the well-validated multi-dimensional human–machine interaction (HMI)2trust measures. As will be shown, this mapping will clarify the terminological chaos and reveal an emergent consensus among the factors that compose cognition with regard to trust in robotics and automation. From there, a review of the experiments which reported reliable and validated regression and plausibly causal models of internal trust will help us to posit a much more complete model of how the cognitive antecedents and factors of trust may be interrelated than has been presented to date.

To minimize confusion and maintain an already established framework in HMI trust, we will be categorizing internal trust along the lines of Hoff and Bashir [60]. They divide such trust into three levels: generic pre-interaction trust attitudes (Dispositional Trust), pre-interaction attitudes towards a specific system given a specified goal(s) and environment (Situational Trust), and attitudes that are learned during or assessed after the interaction (Learned Trust).

## 3 Taking the Current Measure of Trust

## 3.1 Methodology for Assessing Instrument Quality

In order to determine instrument quality, we wanted a method that was flexible enough to accommodate various aspects of trust, multiple styles of instrument and assessment, but still retained reasonable and acceptable standards in the field of psychometric survey creation. To this end, every survey identified was assessed for various forms of reliability and validity and their construction quality.

3.1.1 Reliability. Reliability is the consistency of a test, such as between experimenters (interrater), between points in time (test-retest), between versions of the same test (parallel forms), and between items that purport to measure the same thing (internal consistency). The primary type of reliability we are concerned with here is internal consistency; when multiple questions are asked about the same construct, the responses should be consistent with each other. That being said, if an assessment reported other forms of reliability, it was given credit for having a reliability assessment as other forms of reliability ideally should also be tested and reported.

Within internal consistency, several measures are available, each with its own assumptions that must be acknowledged. The various methods of establishing internal consistency are based on different ways of measuring the correlations between item scores. The simplest is the average inter-item correlation, which should generally be between 0.15 and 0.50. Correlations less than this indicate that the measure is not homogenous (unidimensional); correlations with more than this and the measures may have too much redundancy.

The most common measure is Cronbach’s 𝛼. However, it assumes that factor loadings are equivalent across all survey items, which is not the case for most of the reported scales [39]. Even more critical for avoiding bias in 𝛼 is that the scale is homogeneous (contains a single factor) [39], that the errors for each item are uncorrelated [39], and that there are no missing data, outliers, heavy skew, or other substantial deviations from non-normality [39, 146, 185]. If missing data or non-normality, especially outliers, are concerns, alternative robust calculations for 𝛼 should be used [185]. Care must also be taken to standardize 𝛼 if different items are measured on different scales. Even if all of these assumptions are met, 𝛼 becomes inflated as the number of items increases. Taking all this into account, if Cronbach’s 𝛼 is still used, it should at least be > 0.7 for an experimental scale or > 0.8 for a well-established scale [113]. It should also remain less than < 0.95, or even < 0.9 [160] as too high an alpha indicates redundancy, which can lead to problems with variance inflation if a factor analysis is to be performed. Compared to 𝛼, McDonald’s coefficient omega (𝜔) is a better measure, placing a lower bound on total test reliability while making fewer assumptions. Unfortunately, 𝜔 is under-utilized in the field of measurement in general, especially in trust measures. In part, this may be because there are multiple types of this measure and appropriate thresholds further vary depending on the underlying factors dimensionality [113].

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280"><sup>2</sup>In this work HMI is used to cover all the various fields of HMI including human–computer interaction (HCI), HAI, and HRI. While there may be differences in trust between these areas, this work focuses on their commonality.</span></small>

3.1.2 Statistical Validation. Validation establishes that “the measure of a construct sufficiently measures the intended construct” [119]. Four types of validity were reviewed for each assessment: Statistical Conclusion Validity, Instrument Validity, Content Validity, and Construct Validity.

Statistical Conclusion Validity. It must be demonstrated that the authors gave thought to how to select appropriate items (questions), item wording, and how items co-vary. Researchers must establish the statistical quality and level of their testing and whether they have the appropriate power and sample size for the expected and demonstrated effect sizes and variability. They also should take care in interpreting their results correctly and ensure that the chosen test’s specific assumptions are met. Statistical conclusion validity, however, is insufficient to validate a survey fully, as it can leave potential mediators unaccounted for and relevant variables untested and even conceptually ungrounded. Both instrument and internal validation are also needed.

Instrument Validation. It is vital that researchers develop a clear definition of the construct, both by refining it against the established literature and having subject matter experts (SMEs) review it. Within this process, the goal is to ensure that the construct is neither too broad nor narrow, positively and clearly defined, and that the construct’s nature, domain, entities, and dimensionality are assessed. Not only is it crucial to understand if the construct is unidimensional (homogenous) or multi-dimensional (heterogenous), but also whether the construct is reflective or formative. A reflective construct means that the latent construct is reflected in the items within the instrument. Alternatively, a formative construct is defined by the items composing it. However, it is essential to note that constructs are not inherently formative or reflective and depend on how the construct and indicators are linked, how the researcher understands them, and one’s underlying ontological understanding of the world [87].

Beyond dimensionality and clear language, instrument designers must also carefully consider the item scale (ordinal, nominal, interval, and ratio) and metric type (discrete, continuous). These will affect not only statistical analysis but also the types of questions that can be asked and the resolution at which they can be answered.

Content Validity. In content validation, the primary goal is to ensure conceptual coverage. The items on the survey must be drawn from a universal pool so that the entire construct is covered. SMEs can be leveraged to review the quality of coverage and make sure all aspects of the intended construct are included and no others. More quantitative techniques, such as that of Yao [87], can ensure that individual items are sufficiently unique to maximize coverage while ensuring all construct dimensions are adequately covered.

Construct Validity. Construct validity aims to ensure the construct is being measured and that the results do not arise from methodological quirks and biases. Among other consequences, these biases can artificially inflate or deflate reliability measures, such as 𝛼 and lead to incorrect conclusions about the construction of factors.

Clear, unambiguous language, while basic, is a powerful technique for mitigating systemic bias. Furthermore, acquiescence bias, and even extreme response bias, can be reduced using a mixture of positively and negatively worded items in the same factor [141]. However, factors established from clusters of negatively vs. positively worded items should be handled carefully. Negatively worded items tend to cluster with each other, as do positively worded ones, regardless of latent construct [141]. This problem can be partially mitigated by inverting the direction of the response scale presented to the user instead of using negative wording. This technique protects against acquiescence bias while seemingly serving as less of a threat to response validity [6, 107].

Another commonly encountered issue was factors composed of items sharing similar wording. Such a factor may suffer both from acquiescence bias and the tendency of similarly worded items to cluster together more strongly and have correlated errors. These, in turn, can yield an inflated 𝛼 and lead to invalid factors more generally [107].

Other techniques to validate one particular method are measuring the construct using other modalities and instruments. We looked for evidence that methods such as multitrait-multimethod techniques and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) were used to verify whether convergent validity was achieved or, conversely, discriminant validity [87, 156].

Validity is a complex topic with many facets requiring care to design, develop, and test. Thus, validity cannot be achieved in a single shot but requires iterative refinement of definitions, dimensions, language, items, survey structures, statistical tests, and analysis choices, using both top-down conceptual approaches and bottom-up empirical methods. While some surveys may not have gone through all aspects of this process, others may have simply not reported all steps taken to ensure validity. We kept this in mind while assessing the surveys’ reported reliability and validity, attempting to read them carefully but generously.

## 4 Surveying the Field: Identification of Trust Instruments

Now that we have established how we will assess the various trust instruments in the literature, we must now systematically identify which trust instruments are available to researchers. In this section, we will describe a systematic method for trust assessment identification and the refinement of this list to a tractable number which are sufficiently useful/popular and well documented to perform our in-depth assessment.

## 4.1 Sampling Methodology

To build a sufficient sample, we first collected all trust-related works mentioned among the latest and largest literature reviews across HMI—HCI, HRI, and HAI [13, 41, 53, 61], resulting in 436 records. We added to these 54 other sources that we gathered through our own literature review, especially of more recent works that the reviews may have missed. We then continued to snowball our sample by reviewing these works, especially their background and method sections, and noting all potentially relevant trust studies in these fields. Each time a paper in either literature review mentioned another method/survey instrument, whether used directly or not, that paper was added to the sample, resulting in 687 total records. After accounting for duplication, we also excluded works where no experiment was performed (e.g., review works, theory papers), works that did not use a self-reported trust survey instrument (e.g., those that only measured behavior or physiology), and works to which we did not have full-text access. Other criteria for inclusion were that the work was published in a peer-reviewed venue and accessible in English. We ended up with a sample of 173 experimental works through June 2021.

Then we worked on identifying the trust instruments themselves. Here inclusion criteria were further tightened to instruments developed and used in human-subject studies, and the whole instrument had to be accessible. For instruments published or validated over multiple papers, relevant citations were combined across papers with duplicates removed. In the end, we identified 62 unique survey instruments. This process is outlined in Figure 1.

While we may have missed some trust instruments using this approach, it is unlikely that there remain undiscovered instruments that are widely used. What is more likely is that instruments that are newer or less utilized, such as those primarily in use in a single lab or research group, may have been overlooked. However, the results produced here can be taken as indicative of the trends in the field.

## 4.2 Findings and Down Selection for Analysis

While HMI trust measurement increased gradually starting from the late 1980s, the past decade has seen an explosion in new trust survey instruments, as illustrated in Figure 2. Those HMI trust instruments can be divided into two major classes, those that treat trust as a single factor and those that decompose it along multiple factors, as shown in Figure 3. These classes have about equal representation within the sample.

As illustrated in Figure 3 and Table 1, three very intriguing patterns emerged. First, the popularity of the different instruments varied substantially. Nearly half of the sampled experiments used one of just 12 instruments, and another quarter used either single- or two-item surveys for assessing trust (12.6% and 12.0%, respectively). Fully one-third of experiments opted to develop their own survey, though often incorporating individual questions and even entire factors from the other 62. Over one quarter used one of the other 50 identified instruments wholesale. Thus, while the field exhibits a high degree of variability, certain instruments have proven more impactful than others.

Second, a common finding in our review was the high number of trust instruments were seemingly ad hoc creations. On the other hand, several other instruments were carefully crafted and painstakingly validated. Thus, it became clear that our survey should take on a second, important dimension—to assess the quality of the instruments, as well as their availability and utility.

Third, severe terminological mismatches exist between sub-fields within trust research that have caused further challenges [41, 43, 74, 81]. Taken all together, these patterns indicate there is much competition and critical differences in the field, such that newcomers seeking a trust instrument may need help to choose from among the options. This section will address each of these patterns in turn.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 2. Number of unique multi-item (> 2) HMI trust survey instruments by year published, broken down by the quality of empirical reliability and validity reported.

Most Popular Instruments. The popularity of the extra short single- and two-item assessments is unsurprising given their simplicity and ease of administration. Furthermore, in many applications, trust is only one of several measures being assessed in a study. Keeping the assessments short can reduce the danger of survey fatigue [38] and provide a quick way to probe trust in the moment, making them suitable for inter-task assessments and tasks where time or access to training is limited [73]. On the down side, the biggest weakness of short assessments is their high variance in repeated measures, undermining their reliability. Furthermore, they cannot explain the factors that underlie or lead to trust or lack of it. These and other benefits and pitfalls of such short assessments of trust are given a complete treatment by Körber [73].

The next most popular surveys are the top twelve of the 62 instruments, which accounted for nearly half (47.9%) of citations in the identified literature reviews (Table 1). These findings validate and expand upon those of Brzowski and Nathan-Roberts [13]. The popularity of the majority of these instruments (8) within HRI, in particular, has been confirmed in an independent literature review [70]. The pattern of citations in experimentally-focused HMI papers closely reflected the frequency of usage of each instrument in the literature review, which helps validate that our literature sample statistically reflects the experimental literature overall Table 2. Of these most used 12, McKnight’s and Gefen’s instruments [43, 99] have had the most influence, with the greatest number of general citations both in background and method sections. However, their work also goes far beyond the fields covered in our scope, covering studies of trust in management science, e-commerce, purchasing, and branding, including much work on human-human and human-company trust, though often technologically mediated. and automation literature review. On the other hand, some commonly-cited instruments were barely used in practice (e.g., Fluency [61], SATI [45], CTI [18], Schaefer [138], the German TiA [73]), in part reflecting the deep divisions and lack of overlap between even the seemingly closely related fields that study human-machine trust, such as fluency, automation trust, e-commerce, and HCI.

Assessing Instrument Quality. To assess the current quality of field surveys, we classified them by the quality of their internal reliability and quantitative validity. As discussed above (Section 3.1.1), internal reliability can be calculated in many ways. While the standard is Cronbach’s 𝛼, reporting it alone is insufficient to establish the test’s reliability unless its assumptions are met. This is true of all the internal reliability tests; researchers must account for sample size, missing data, outliers, skew, kurtosis, heterogeneity, and 𝜏-equivalence. Reporting more than one test also increases confidence that the reliability is accurate. Thus, we understood a test to have Complete Reliability if it reported internal reliability and checked that the data met the test’s assumptions.

For validity, the gold standard is a complete exploratory factor analysis, including reporting the number of subjects, rotation used, factor loadings, justified choice of factor number, and descriptive statistics - especially including the number of items per factor. Failing this, however, a CFA then it was considered sufficiently complete if it included root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) and at least two fit statistics such as $\chi ^ { 2 }$ , the standardized root mean square residual (SRMR), the comparative fit index (CFI), or the Tucker-Lewis index (TLI). Instruments meeting all appropriate minimally sufficient criteria were classified as reporting Complete Reliability and Validity. If some of these elements were missing, but more effort was made and reported than Cronbach reliability alone, the instrument was categorized as having Some Reliability and Validity. Those that reported no reliability or validity analysis or only Cronbach’s internal reliability were classified as No Reliability or Validity.

It is important to note that carrying out appropriate analyses alone does not mean that the results met any acceptable thresholds, however. Criteria for assessing the actual quality of the validity and reliability are discussed below in Section §10.1. Furthermore, while we have done our best to identify the most influential and best-validated instruments currently, this is liable to change.

Many of the 62 instruments, especially those that measure trust as a single factor, lack reported reliability or validity (Figure 3), with 24% having no validity or reliability analysis of any sort and another 24% only reporting Cronbach’s 𝛼 for internal reliability. Only 17% of studies with a singlefactor instrument report any level of both empirical validity and reliability analyses, compared to 54% of multi-factor instruments. This is unsurprising, given that multi-factor instruments are subjected to greater scrutiny of dimensional validity. Even so, 30% of multi-factor surveys did not report any reliability and validity testing (Figure 3). Despite repeated calls for stronger instrument validation [43, 73], the number of studies utilizing instruments without validation has increased over the last decade. However, there are currently some promising signs of that trend reversing (see the most recent years in Figure 2).

It is worth noting a particular tradeoff in types of validity evident throughout our review, lack of survey reuse. Among those that used or incorporated other surveys, only 17% used other trust instruments wholesale. In contrast, the remainder used other previously validated instruments to get at specific individual antecedents or trust-related factors. Reusing surveys allows for direct comparison and can help validate the reliability and generalizability of an instrument. On the other hand, creating new surveys can help confirm the nomological/construct validity of both the new survey and the parallel constructs in previous works [12].

The most common of these were instruments that aim to capture one’s disposition to trust without regard to a specific system or goal, such as Faith in Technology or Faith in People. Faith in Technology was most often captured with the complacency potential rating scale (CPRS) [148] (4 studies) or the Negative Attitudes Toward Robots Scale [118] (6 studies). Faith in People was measured with instruments like Rotter’s Interpersonal Trust Scale [135], or the instruments of Moorman, Deshpande, and Zaltman [110], McShane and von Glinow [103], Wheeles and Grotz [177], and Anderson and Dedrick [3]. The next most common area to try and capture independently are assessments of trust antecedents or correlates such as likeability, bonding, human likeness/anthropomorphism, or affect [23, 57, 67, 104, 166, 174]. Other areas measured included Suspicion [86, 143], Situation Awareness [26], Mood [123], Risk [29, 123, 127], Transparency [137], and Intention to Work [35]. Finally, Workload, both with the NASA task load index (TLX) and other measures, was the most popular non-trust-related measure (12 studies).

Terminology Challenges. Upon first inspection, there appears to be little overlap with how various instruments decompose trust and, thus, how they assess it. Further probing reveals that a conceptual consensus is emerging behind the terminological differences. The following section in this chapter will work to provide a unifying language and then apply that language to the selection of papers chosen so that a complete understanding and comparison can be made.

## 5 Mapping and Defining the Factors and Antecedents of Human Machine Trust

Thus, between the bottom-up analysis of individual items and the clustering of commonalities between the reliable and validated multi-factorial survey instruments, we ultimately grouped each set of identified categories as cleanly as possible into ten factors. A mapping of the reliable and validated factors from the sampled surveys is displayed in Tables 3 and 4. The purpose of this is to primarily show that despite the vast diversity in terminology and dozens of varying survey instruments coming from a multiplicity of fields and approaches, the measurement of trust across human-system interaction is converging.

Furthermore, the subsequent section takes those ten factors and maps them to the tripartite framework of Hoff and Bashir [60]. This categorization was done to ensure consistency and clarity within the existing trust literature, in which the Hoff and Bashir framework is well known and often cited. mappings to their three levels of Dispositional, Situational and Learned Trust as defined in at the end of Section 2.

One point that we had to consider, though, was which factors could be considered antecedents instead of direct or proper trust factors. This is a complex question, as different approaches and definitions treat trust differently. For some, Faith in Technology would be considered a proper trust factor [58, 104, 148]. Others might consider Shared Mental Model one instead [137, 178]. Herein, because many in the field want to differentiate between antecedents of trust and trust itself, the choice was made to name those factors that are more downstream, per the meta-analysis in Section 7, as more direct factors of trust and more upstream ones as antecedents. Shared Mental Model is broken out of from the three layer model of Hoff and Bashir and stands between the antecedents layers (Dispositional, Situational) and what some call ‘proper’ trust (i.e., Learned Trust), wherein each factor can be described as an expectation. As will be explained further below, the antecedent factors can be understood as feeding into the holistic Shared Mental Model, which in turn serves as a foundation for forming the expectations that compose the factors of Learned Trust.

In order to further exploit the increased cross-discipline understandability this convergence makes possible, and for greater lucidity in this paper, we will now proceed to describe each of these critical factors for understanding human-machine trust. The following factors are the most commonly found to be distinct, reliable, and have multiple forms of validity (i.e., surface, construct, internal, and external). We do not claim these constructs are perfect or that the terms we have chosen are the best. However, we believe they capture the emergent consensus among the experimental literature and the collected measures.

## 5.1 Dispositional Level

The term Dispositional<sup>3</sup> herein refers to beliefs or attitudes that exist before one is considering or in a particular situation or interaction; we still recognize that this level may be composed of multiple distinct factors. While there may be many components, they generally fall along three lines: faith in persons, faith in institutions, and faith in technology. These are not natural dispositions in the same sense that Hoff and Bashir employed the term [60] but are generic attitudes. Some of the oldest multi-item trust measurement instruments were those measuring faith in institutions and persons [135, 150]. However, these surveys have rarely been used in conjunction with HMI research.

On the other hand, faith in technology is relatively common, appearing as a factor within 10/25 reliable and validated multi-factor surveys (see Tables 5 and 6). Just because Dispositional factors are not in the Learned trust layer, that does not mean they, or those in the Situational level, are static. They may get updated but at much slower time scales than Learned trust, as previous interactions shape future dispositions, sense of situation normality, familiarity, and future emotional responses.

5.1.1 Faith in Technology. This factor is defined by how much faith one has in technology. While sometimes it is with regard to a specific area of technology, such as humanoid robots or autonomous cars, more often it is assessed generally, such as asking users whether technology makes their life better. Faith in technology is a form of dispositional trust, that is, it is not particular to the given situation or even technology involved but one’s general trust, though it may be specific to a given type of technology or socio-technical interaction (e.g., robots, online shopping, and automation). While this can be thought of as a form of trust, in terms of a given trust interaction, this is more of a trust antecedent or prior that may indicate how a person will feel and what they may anticipate upon first encountering a specific system. We also choose to term it faith, in alignment with [99], to stress that it may not be based on any evidence or experience.

Faith in Technology is also called Propensity to Trust Machines [148], Trusting Stance, or simply Faith [99], Attitude [57, 117, 142], and Anxiety [57, 118] (see Table 3). It is often measured with pre-existing Dispositional trust survey instruments aimed at capturing attitudes and anxiety toward robots or automation, such as the CPRS [148]. One validated standalone variant of this factor that specifically looks at faith in technology from the view of high expectations of technology and all-or-none thinking is the Perfect Automation Schema [107]. If the questions are left open about a generic “robot,” then this factor may also include the Robot Anxiety Scale and the Negative Attitude toward Robots Scale [117]. However, those scales may correspond more closely to Emotional response, below, if measured within a specific situation or interaction. Given the wide range of facets that the dispositional may capture, one outstanding question is whether this factor is homogeneous.

## 5.2 Situational Level

Situational factors are those that are contextually relevant to the specific situation or interaction but exist prior to the current interaction. These draw upon previous knowledge or experience with elements of the system at hand (familiarity), similar systems (situation normality), and what the design of the system or the quality of the interaction evoke (emotional response). These all inform the mental model the user formulates of the system, its goals, capabilities, preferences, and procedures. Situational factors are not normally considered forms of trust in and of themselves but as their antecedents.

5.2.1 Familiarity. At the heart of the situational antecedents stands familiarity, which is not only about indirect knowledge but also includes direct experience with the vendor, product, or brand. The first part of familiarity includes indirect acquaintance such as reputation, recommendation, and Social Influence [73]. These sub-factors are central to Familiarity in human-human trust [182] and marketing [48], though mostly ignored in HMI. It is primarily termed familiarity by most surveys that employ it, except for Scopelliti’s somewhat confusingly named category: Capabilities of Robots [142], as shown in Table 3. This factor may be overlooked when trust is measured for users interacting with newly developed systems, especially in academic settings, given the technologies lack of branding and novelty.

5.2.2 Situation Normality. In such cases, it may be preferable to focus on Situation normality, which is similar to familiarity but more indirect. Similar experiences with other technologies or machine behaviors and functionalities create recognizable parallels from which the human’s expectations are formed. This is a well-known phenomenon across technological trust domains from information system software [82, 98], eCommerce [43, 72], and automation [83]. Per Table 3, it is usually referred to as Situation(al) Normality [42, 43, 99, 121] but sometimes construed under life-likeness [126], in a limited functional/behavioral sense. The relation between life-likeness and situation normality is underscored by how the latter is mediated by anthropomorphism [183].

5.2.3 Emotional Response. Defining the appropriate scope of this category and naming it required much thought, and its cohesiveness as a single factor requires further substantiation. The unique name of this category is based on the increasing acceptance of the term emotive to describe the response evoked by robots when studying these factors in relation to trust [41, 45, 66, 68, 138]. This category spans factors such as warm [79], sociable [57, 126], pleasant, friendly, likeable [104, 128], evoking of comfort, and attachment [17, 89], engagement [121], seriousness [49], dominance [126], and professionalism [149] (see Table 3). Related but negatively valenced factors exist may be anxiety [118], and more general negative attitudes [117] when measured once a situation has been initiated.

The importance of emotional response has been increasingly acknowledged by HRI, especially in affective robotics [91, 104, 138]. Anthropomorphism likely affects trust through this antecedent, as does the user interface more generally [28, 54, 183]. Note that we chose Emotional response as it focuses on the human’s internal psychological assessment and reaction as opposed to the physical or functional properties of the system being interacted with, which better encompasses the factors among the survey instruments.

## 5.3 Shared Mental Model

Shared Mental Model (SMM) was chosen as an existing term that broadly captures one’s perception of a system’s understanding of their interaction and the (lack of) confidence that brings about. This category has seen the highest variability due to construct proliferation and poor un derstanding. Consequently, our naming schema deviates more from those currently used as this concept than the other categories. As illustrated in Table 3, it has been variously called: Perceived Understandability/Technical Competence[89], Intention of Developers+Understanding/Predictability [73], Responsiveness [126], Process Transparency [18], Intentionality [165], Comfort of Use and Transparency [49], Process [121, 151], Understanding [178], Wearable Technology Trust [137], Perceived Ease of Use [8, 43, 58], and, perhaps most confusingly, HRI [142].

While similar, the Shared Mental Model can be thought of as a subset of a theory of mind system which infers cognitive states. It specifically is the part which models the trustee’s understanding of the trustor’s goals, methodological preferences, their relationship and interaction, and what the trustor believes the trustee knows of them personally. The inferred cognitive states that a shared mental model embedded in a theory of mind support can be termed Situation Awareness [4, 158]. Shared Mental Models are the infrastructure that allow Situation Awareness but match the factors among the survey literature more clearly, and SMMs themselves are not as directly tied to predictability [158] The formation of a Shared Mental Model on the current perceived state of the interaction yields the ‘highest’ level of Situation Awareness, the ability to project how the situation will unfold into the future [4, 158]. However, the SMM itself does not include predictability but serves as an antecedent to it [4]. This is in line with the literature which supports that in trust measurement predictability itself is more strongly correlated with Capability-based Trust [99, 153, 163].

The shared term was included to stay consistent with previous works [4, 132, 138]. More im portantly, it emphasizes that this mental model focuses on the overlapping knowledge and joint goals needed to complete shared teamwork and task work [4]. Shared mental models support coordination, collaboration, and interdependence whereas mental model alone is focused on the atomized individual [139]. It also is intended to account for the trustor’s mental model incorporating their beliefs about the trustee’s mental model [7].

While here we categorized it as an antecedent of trust, it seems to exist between situational and learned trust. The shared mental model is initially formed by the dispositional and situational levels but, unlike them, gets quickly and continuously updated during the trust interaction as one learns more [158].

## 5.4 Learned Trust

Within the Learned level, we are now talking about forms of actual trust and no longer antecedents. As such, all of these factors directly have trust in their names. These are factors that continuously are re-assessed in the interaction as it dynamically progresses between the system and the human and appears to be composed of four main factors.

5.4.1 Structural Trust. This factor is defined as the belief that the trustee will abide by whatever cultural and behavioral norms, morals, agreements, and laws the trustor expects. Structural Trust includes the motivations of the trustee to follow such norms, including having a sense of integrity, responsibility, honor, and shame. This factor has also been termed Reliance [148], in addition to Credibility-Character [128], Fairness [165], Honesty [165], and Integrity [8, 95] (see

Table 4). This type of trust is closely related to perceived moral agency [5], though that is more about the capacity for morality than the trust placed in shared norms. Hence, why the author of that study depended on [133] to measure trust separately. While an instrument designed for human-human interpersonal trust, [133] can be understood as specifically focusing on the shared mental model, structural, and affective trust.

We specifically chose the word trust within the factor name to differentiate from assurance, integrity, honesty, and fairness. It is not Structural Assurance, which only focuses on regulatory and institutional mechanisms [42, 43, 99, 121], and does not also include beliefs about the trustee’s motives or likelihood of compliance with structural mechanisms. The latter is well-captured by Mayer’s Integrity [95] but that term purposely was chosen to exclude external, institutional mechanisms. The additional aspect of Structural Assurance integrates a normative framing, while remaining open to both internally and externally driven motives. In additional to allowing for external motivations, we also choose to call this a type of trust, whereas integrity, as well as terms like honesty and fairness, are ambiguous as to whether they refer to beliefs of the trustor or properties of the trustee (i.e., their trustworthiness) and tend to be strongly anthropomorphic. Structural trust is therefore more amenable both being more commensurate to non-human trustees and by placing the focus on the trustor’s perception of the trustee.

5.4.2 Capability-based Trust. This category, whose name is based on [42], broadly captures whether a system has the resources and capabilities to perform a task (competence) [8, 71, 73], one’s belief in that competence, whether based on experience or faith (confidence) [65, 77, 78], the belief that the system performs the task reliably (reliance) [73, 89, 99, 164, 165], and that the system can recover from errors (robustness) [45, 89] Depending on the system, security, privacy, and accessibility may all be perceived as falling under Capability-based Trust, though they are sometimes more accurately framed as elements of Structural Trust. Other factors that may capture all or part of these concepts, per Table 4, are usefulness [43, 56, 57], attitude [57], functionality [99, 138, 164], performance [18, 121, 138, 151, 178], fluency [61], robot-relative contribution [61], and capable [165]. Some surveys take all trust or trustworthiness as capability-based and term the factor accordingly [17, 106, 148]. Capability-based Trust is similar to Mayer’s Ability factor, except we once again use the term trust in the name to make it clear that this is a direct form of trust, as opposed to an antecedent, and that this is not a property of the trustee. Instead, it is a trust based on the trustee’s capability as perceived or expected by the trustor.

Another common but confusing term for this factor is cognitive or cognition-based trust [64, 71, 138, 163], as all trust emerges from cognition. This usage rested on the assumption that cognitive trust was evidence-based and rationally derived as opposed to affective trust arising from blind emotions [81]. This division is based on the philosophical understanding that one form of trust is irrational because it is tied to emotions. However, the debates over the rationality of emotions [24, 47, 53, 124, 154] and cognition as computation [125, 167] are long standing. Thus, despite less historical weight, we chose the term capability-based trust over cognition-based or cognitive trust. However, we retained the term affective trust, as explained below.

5.4.3 Affective Trust. Affective trust is the belief that the trustee will support one’s goals or actions to achieve those goals. More generally, it may be understood as how cooperative the trustee is expected to be [31, 44, 101]. At its most narrow, this factor has been termed Calculative-Based Beliefs [43] and at its broadest and most anthropomorphized, benevolence [8, 18, 95, 169]. Between the two we find Purpose [18, 121, 151], Intention of Developers [73], Safety [148], Goal [61], and Helpfulness [99, 153, 163, 176], as seen in Table 4. Despite the popularity of Mayer’s trust definition [95], we caution against framing this factor as benevolence, which may imply that the robot or machine is kind, caring, and capable of goodwill. As was the case with Integrity vs. Structural Trust, we took pains to avoid over-anthropomorphication.

Concepts such as honesty and loyalty may sometimes be construed as either Affective or Structural, or a mix of both. Their categorization is affected by perceived motivation, such as whether the robot is enabling one’s goals because it is aware of them specifically or because it is conforming to societal standards. Depending on the questions asked, these two constructs may overlap so heavily as to be indistinguishable and be captured under the catch-all term relation-based trust [76]. Conversely, their opposites may be packed together into an amorphous distrust category that includes deception, trickiness, and underhandedness, like the distrust items in [63]. In general, distrust is often meant as the antonym of Affective Trust, which may lead to confusion as to whether it is the opposite of ‘trust’ or whether it is a distinct concept that must be measured independently [80]. The potentiality for conflation between these two constructs is seen in the closely related challenge of defining alignment, as discussed below in Sec. 8.2.

Another limitation of our goal-supportive definition is that it can be at odds with a more dyadic, Affective trust that the trustee wants what is best for the trustor. This can lead to a paternalistic tension between the trustor’s self-posited goals and intended means and the trustee’s belief in what the trustor should want or how they should act. As we are primarily interested in goal-focused trust, for now, we simply acknowledge that this can lead to different conceptions of affective trust, especially across cultures where paternalism may be received very differently [21, 69, 122, 147].

5.4.4 General Trust. This category probes trust or trustworthiness directly, though questions can range from focusing on a particular function to the whole system. Questions here also may ask about trust in those that designed, built, or sold the system. Per Table 4, other monikers for this category include Trust in (Service) Robots [61, 121], Trust in Automation [73], Trusting Beliefs in Specific Technologies [99], Perceived Machine Accuracy [104], Social Service Robot Interaction Trust [17], and simply Trust [42, 58, 151].

5.4.5 Intent to Use. Once we get beyond evaluating all our other internal beliefs, perceived risk, and other environmental and task-related factors, we must finally decide whether to trust. It is usually called some variation of Intention [8, 42, 57, 58, 99, 121], but also sometimes Reliance [104] or Confidence [18, 148] (see Table 4), which some may find particularly confusing.

## 6 Final Selection of Studies to Analyze

It is simply beyond the scope of this dissertation to thoroughly analyze for validity, reliability, and terminology used in all 62 instruments. Instead, a down-selection was performed, it quickly became clear that despite the wide number of instruments only around a dozen were cited frequently or re-utilized among the validated reports, as discussed above in Section 4.2.

As many papers cite these works, totals in Table 2 should be taken as estimates of upper bounds on the number of relevant papers. Here the citations among Method sections, according to Semantic Scholar, best reflect unique experiments, so we can likely put the upper bound on experiments that cite these Top 12 at ∼ 1, 500. Assuming our sampling method was appropriate, this represents approximately half of the total experiments, so there are likely 3000 relevant experiments, of which our literature review analyzed 173 (5.7%). At this sample size, we can have 95% confidence that the Top 12 really do represent approximately 50 ± 7.2% of all survey instruments used in experimental research.

While there are other contenders for top spots as far as direct experimental usage, these 12 were identified and chosen to analyze herein after assessing their overall impact (as partially illustrated in Table 2). This list is by no means exhaustive, and the choice of 12 was made primarily to scope our study. However, we believe they represent a substantial sample of the current state-of-the-art, a good range of validated factors, and provide an entry point into assessing how instruments are tested for reliability and validity.

With these definitions of trust and its antecedents in mind, we can now turn to the Top 12 trust instruments and assess their reliability and validity as well as how well they cover these major internal categories that relate to the psychology of trust and its antecedents. Note that these categories did not include external environmental, or robot-based factors, but were limited to what the human perceives, understands, and expects of the robot.

## 7 The Structure of Human-Machine Trust

The inter-relations between these ten antecedents and trust factors was further refined and validated by closely examining the 15 studies that performed regressions and structural equation modeling. The names, sample size, and factor coverage of each of these studies is given in Table 6, whereas the details of the reported regression coefficients between each factor in each survey can be found in Appendix A: Table 9. While not every study tested every factor, the meta-analysis presented in Table 7 reveals some general trends that suggest a common set of relationships, if not an underlying joint structure.

As can be seen in Table 7 at the Dispositional trust level, Faith in Technology has the strongest effect on the Shared Mental Model, followed by Structural and Capability-based Trust, General Trust, Situational Normality, and finally, and most weakly, on Intention to Use. Its effect weakens over the interaction [106] and over repeated interactions [153] as one gets used to a specific technology and better calibrates their trust. Thinking about trust as a Bayesian expectation (such as in [65]), Faith in Technology essentially serves as an initial prior belief whose contribution diminishes over time. Therefore, Faith in Technology is most crucial at the initial stages of trust formation, when potential users decide whether to accept and try out new technology. Faith in Technology gets updated through feedback as both General Trust, and the Shared Mental Model more generally, are calibrated [57, 60].

The factors within the Situational trust level, similar to those in the Dispositional level, show larger effects early on that diminish overuse [106]. Likeability can even account entirely for early usage of a system until trust is calibrated [104]. Emotional Response is significantly correlated (partial corr: $0 . 5 4 , \mathrm { S E } \mathrm { : } 0 . 1 3 \; p < 0 . 0 1 )$ with Situation Normality [57]. This relationship, perhaps, is best exemplified by anthropomorphism, which increases naturalness, likeability, and comfort that all directly impact Situation Normality [17]. Likewise, there is some evidence that Situation Normality increases comfort and attachment [17]. Situation Normality and Emotional Response both appear to be significant and fairly strong antecedents (partial corr: $0 . 3 3 \mathrm { - } 0 . 4 7 ,   p < 0 . 1 )$ to more ‘downstream’ factors such as the Shared Mental Model, General Trust, and Intent to Use. Familiarity, on the other hand, seems somewhat weaker (partial corr: $0 . 1 { - } 0 . 4 2 ,   p < 0 . 1 )$ , perhaps some of its explanatory power being divided with Situation Normality. It appears plausible from the structural equation models (SEMs) that Familiarity primarily affects the Shared Mental Model, and through that, the sub-factors of trust (Affective, Structural, Capability-based), and eventually Intent to Use. Few experiments [17, 57] have separately tested the sub-factors of reputation and recommendation, for which there are mixed results from the human-human side [182]. Because the above strength of Situational Trust factors weaken over experience, their effect on Intent to Use and actual use may be underestimated or exhibit higher variance, depending on the point in time at which they are measured.

The Shared Mental Model sits at the foundation of Learned trust and is crucial in supporting Capability-based (partial corr adj:0.42, SE 0.03, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 0 1 )$ and General Trust (partial corr $adj: 0.52, SE  0.02, p < 0.00001)$ . Like other Learned trust factors, the Shared Mental Model gets calibrated over time and is correlated with transparency and the ability to monitor (and thus is also

affected by workload [132]). At the crux of the Shared Mental Model is recognizing the goals of the robot [61, 162] and the developers’ intentions [73], such that one can determine if the robot or machine shares the human’s goals or at least is cooperative vs. competitive [15]. Likewise, the Shared Mental Model is equally necessary for determining whether another will follow laws or norms and hence warrant Structural Trust [130].

Affective trust is the foundation of the main trust factors, indicating expected cooperativeness and goal adoption. Expected cooperativeness vs. competitiveness is critical to understanding whether the potential actors and situation call for trust [131], while goal adoption is the very purpose of task-focused interpersonal trust [15]. Affective Trust correlates with both Structural (partial corr: 0.43, SE: 0.08, $\bar { p } < 0 . 0 1 )$ and Capability-based Trust (partial corr: $0 . 6 6 , \mathrm { S E } : 0 . 0 4 , p = 0 . 0 0 3 5 )$ as well as General Trust (partial corr: 0.37, SE: 0.01, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 0 1 )$ . The extent literature remains unclear as to how Learned Affective Trust is formed or what its antecedents are, though it may be directly shaped Dispositionally [138, 163].

Despite its relative lack of attention in the HMI trust literature, the effect of Structural Trust on General Trust has proven surprisingly strong (partial corr:0.40, SE: 0.02, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 0 1 )$ . Its strength may be an indication that, indeed, ethics and integrity are relevant to specific robotics applications in contradiction to earlier suppositions [19]. While Structural Trust’s importance may be application specific, the minor variance across experiments in its effective strength indicates otherwise. However, Structural Trust may have a weaker effect on Intent to Use (partial corr: 0.12, SE: 0.10, $\bar { p } < 0 . 1 )$ because it gets over-ridden by other factors (e.g., Capability-based Trust, workload) [19].

Capability-based Trust is usually the go-to in HMI; however, these results indicate that focusing on it alone may be a mistake. Capability-based Trust is only marginally more strongly correlated with General Trust (partial corr: 0.47, SE: 0.01, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 0 1 )$ than Structural (partial corr: 0.40, SE: 0.02, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 0 1 )$ or Affective Trust (partial corr: 0.37, SE: 0.01, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 1$ ). On the other hand, Capability-based Trust has a much stronger direct effect on Intent to Use (partial corr adj: 0.33, SE: 0.05, $p = 0 . 0 0 0 9 )$ . It also becomes increasingly important over time, replacing the effects of Dispositional and Situational Trust [106]. Many instruments found that Capability-based Trust encompassed two distinct sub-factors, often called Performance and Reliability. The former can be defined as one’s belief in another’s ability, while the latter is their confidence assessment of that belief. For example, I may think that a machine is accurate 80% of the time, but I may only be 30% sure that I am correct. How these beliefs may be combined into a singular assessment is another matter (two ways forward may be Dempster-Shafer Theory or Subjective Logic [65]). A similar dichotomy between expectation and confidence may be paralleled in Structural Trust with the sub-groupings of Ethical and Sincere, respectively [76]. While no survey has yet demonstrated a similar dichotomy in Affective Trust, the linguistic cluster analysis in [63] suggests that Wariness may serve as the inverse of confidence in Affective Trust.

While General Trust does not fully determine Intent to Use, it is strongly correlated with it (partial corr adj: 0.63, SE: 0.01, $p < 0 . 0 0 0 0 1 )$ . While strong, this amount of correlation reinforces that Intent to Use is not just a matter of trusting beliefs but is affected by a range of external factors, such as cognitive workload and perceived risk [29].

## 8 Discussion

## 8.1 Structure of HRI Trust—An Emergent Model

The meta-analysis reveals a convergent picture of HMI Trust emerging out of the efforts of many researchers. Figure 4 provides a graphical summary of this emergent model of trust. As can be seen, the trust factors and antecedents can be fairly neatly grouped into three layers, substantiating the early findings of Hoff and Bashir [60]. The overall direction of plausible causality and strong intersurvey agreement has revealed a tentative picture of trust that is, in many ways, intuitive. A priori Dispositional expectations are first filtered through contextual, Situational trust antecedents such as one’s Familiarity with the system, its similarity to previous systems (Situational Normality), and one’s impression of the system (Emotional Response). These antecedents all feed into one’s Shared Mental Model of the system, which then supports three different types of expectations - whether the system shares the user’s goal (Affective), whether it is Capable of achieving that goal, and whether it will follow expected norms or laws when trying to achieve that goal (Structural). They all contribute to a General assessment of trust, which in turn influences their Intent to Use the system. Additional studies have further bolstered this model, especially regarding the dynamics of trust over time. Throughout the interaction, the higher-level factors play decreasingly important roles, as the Shared Mental Model gets updated and the learned trust factors calibrate more closely to external circumstances.

## 8.2 Are the Differences between Affective and Structural Trust Substantial Enough to Merit Separate Categories?

The best way to conceive of Structural Trust is to go back to Luhmann [84], the originator of the whole science of trust. Structural, or what he called societal trust, is the abstraction of Affective, or personal, trust. Affective Trust is founded in the dyadic trust relationship, is rooted in personal knowledge, and is realized through individual attachment, bond, loyalty, and love. In contrast, Structural Trust universalized this in a world of strangers.

Thus, while the two are related and both fall under relation-based trust [76], there are also fundamental differences between Structural and Affective Trust. Affective Trust is driven by the particular, recognizing the individual’s specific goals and supporting them. In human-human trust, this can be out of benevolence, loyalty, love, or attachment. However, we have contended that these sources for Affective Trust are not essential, especially in the human-machine context [131]. Instead, we can understand it as arising from inter-agent expectations of commitment and cooperation to achieve shared goals. On the other hand, Structural Trust is about fairness and equality of treatment. In humans, it may be driven by fear of sanction or internally-driven honor or integrity to uphold universal norms [31], and in general, is about how power dynamics encourage compliance around how goals are achieved [131].

That being said, as one factor is derived from the other, the difference between them may not always be so clear, as is illustrated by the correlation between Affective and Structural Trust. This is because it can be unclear whether honesty, loyalty, and respect should be situated as Affective or Structural. How one differentiates these concepts can depend on cultural understanding, personal motivations, ethical framing, and whether they are attributed to internal or external motivations [18, 31, 90].

The challenge of differentiating between these two factors can be seen in the parallel challenge of defining alignment. Alignment has been variously defined as

—(Provably) aligning the values/goals/intentions of robots/AI with those of humans [9, 62, 108, 179] and [Russell, per 145]

— “A is aligned with H if A is trying to do what H wants it to do” [20]

—Ensuring that the AI agent’s outer and inner objectives of align with human values. The outer objectives are those defined by AI designers based on human values, while the inner objectives are those optimized within AI agents. [145]

These varied definitions highlight the tension between whether the alignment is with an individual or a group. This tension has led some researchers to differentiate between more general structural normative alignment and personalized value alignment [9]. These definitions also reveal a potential difference between alignment and trust - whose values, even when we only consider individuals, are we trying to align with - the designers or the users?

A common question arises as to whether Affective and Structural Trust are both worth measuring<sup>4</sup>, as many may not see how they are relevant to a specific robot pick-and-place task in a lab, for example. That the robot could be nefarious and have competitive goals (Affective Trust) or not follow the rules (Structural Trust) is often not even considered. Asking about deception can, in fact, elicit suspicion in both of these categories, an issue to which we will return. Affective Trust is likely always at play, even if it is only in the narrowest calculative-based sense, i.e., [43]. Ignoring Structural Trust in the lab presents a severe threat to etiological validity where it may have clear effects on behavior and beliefs in the real world when it comes to branding; attitudes toward tech companies, government, and industry regulations; and insurance liability. Furthermore, AIs and robots are assumed to be more fair and ethical than humans [155], demonstrating potential bias in Structural Trust.

Another reason to differentiate between Affective, Structural, and Capability-based trust is that antecedent factors have different effects on them. For instance, Structural Trust is directly affected by Dispositional factors, whereas Affective Trust does not seem to be. We rely on structural assurance to protect us from strangers and new technologies, linking Faith in Technology and Structural Trust. Another example of the differential effect of antecedents was found in our own experiments [129], where Familiarity affected Capability-based Trust but not Structural. By dividing out the factors that compose trust, we can better understand which antecedents affect which aspects of our expectations and better understand the internal dynamics of trust.
