## 8.3 Comparison with Human-Human Trust Measurement

Unlike HMI trust, early works on human-human trust were entirely focused on Dispositional trust measures [44, 97, 135]. Measures for inter-personal trust started developing in many professional contexts, from organizational trust between employees and managers, between firms, and within business networks [10, 64, 95, 140]. A second major approach developed that studied trust in friendships and intimate relationships [14, 46]. Building off these approaches, other veins developed in the healthcare community between patients and doctors [3, 161], as well as trust in media [93], and trust in strangers [36].

While HMI trust rarely explored Faith in People or Faith in Technology Companies, it did occasionally employ or adapt questions from human-human works (e.g., [61, 91, 95, 135, 177]), though generally did not incorporate them into their larger model or show that they correlated with other antecedents or trust factors. Human-human trust work should also be credited for dividing out Affective from Capability-based Trust [81], as well as Structural Assurance from Situational Normality [101]. Many still cite or even test with the Interpersonal Trust Scale [135], and the influence of Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman [95], who primarily worked in organizational trust, is hard to overstate. The latter is cited in approximately half of all HMI trust scales and in almost every major literature review and is one of the most influential models across human-human trust research [97].

An essential point of comparison to this study is McEvily and Tortoriello [97], who performed a similar review for human-human trust scales. They identified around the same number of trust scales in human-human trust as this study and found a similar pattern of development, where 60% had created their own ad hoc measures, and 40% re-used a previously validated instrument. They also discussed the reliability and construct validity patterns over time. During their review, they found that even fewer human-human scales had reported empirical validity measures than we found for HMI scales. Furthermore, only 22% of human-human scales considered multi-factorial trust as opposed to single uni-dimensional items.

The factors and antecedents reported fall closely in line with our own, as seen in Table 8.

Beyond analogous factors, the similarity in structure is more than apparent. This resemblance lends support to the model of CASAs [115], though the internal weights or expectations assigned to individual factors may indeed differ [28].

One important supporting pattern of convergence is that we found Learned Trust to be composed of three primary sub-factors: Capability-based Trust, Affective Trust, and Structural

Trust, closely paralleling Mayer’s Ability, Benevolence, and Integrity [94, 95] We deliberately chose different terminology to avoid over-anthropomorphication and stressing that we are not focusing on properties of the trustee but the perceptions of the trustor. We also have important differences in nuance, especially with regard to monitoring and the role of institutional mechanisms in bringing about structural assurance.

There was only one major grouping that our model did not capture, which was how “available, open, and receptive” the potential trustees and trustors were. Likely, this grouping is closely tied to the importance of Agreeableness in trust from Personality research [40], as well as our factor of Emotional Response. However, it seems distinct enough within human-human trust to merit its own factor and a potential focus of future work in HMI. On the other hand, Shared Mental Models were entirely missing in McEvily Tortoriello [97]. However, while a decade ago, human-human trust may have lacked such measures, the importance of this factor in human-human trust is now being recognized (e.g., [96]). While many have considered the differences between human-human and human-robot trust [2, 28, 86, 88], the relevant factors and their measurement are highly similar, and we hope that works like this one will continue to bridge the gap.

## 9 Outstanding Issues

## 9.1 Modelling Limitations

As this is a meta-analysis where not every survey covered every factor, many factors were not assessed for their potential as mediating factors. Furthermore, of the 29 relationships examined, 15 are only supported by a single source in our sample, 5 by two sources, and only 9 have three or more sources. Of those 9, 7 exhibit high heterogeneity, making it challenging to identify which values are outliers or to detect certain biases. There are also 5 relationships whose lower confidence interval bounds cross 0, which threatens their significance level. Additionally, there are two relationships where the standard error is nearly as large as, if not larger than, the partial correlation. Finally, there are three relationships (see blue dashed arrows in Figure 4) where the plausible direction of causality is reversed in one source compared to all other surveys. Many of these relationships require further repeated testing with reliable and valid instruments over large samples to clarify their significance and plausible direction.

Another challenge is correctly understanding what SEMs imply and do not imply with regard to causality. There are many misunderstandings about SEMs, and it should be understood that SEMs do not prove causality. However, if the assumptions of SEMs and statistical measures of fit prove sufficient, then evidence for the plausibility of causality [11] is gained. While we combine SEM and regression results in the meta-analysis, it is also worthwhile to clarify that SEM and regression are not the same, as SEM incorporates causally-relevant assumptions [11]. This does not preclude combining them in a meta-analysis, but we can no longer assume those assumptions hold.

Another issue can arise with modeling; too few questions may be asked to establish individual factors. This issue caused us to not include 3 reliable and valid instruments in our meta-analysis. For example, single Affective trust items focusing on cooperativeness, shared goals, and benevolence often cluster with Calculative-based factors due to their high correlation (partial corr:0.66, SE 0.04) when an insufficient number of questions on Affective trust are asked (e.g., [138]). This merger is especially true for surveys that treat trust as a single factor, for instance Rupp et al.’s use of Jian [137].

## 9.2 External Trust Factors

While the canvassed surveys converge on the trust model presented above, there is good reason to believe from numerous experiments that other factors also impact trust. While the literature has explored dozens of potential factors and antecdents [50, 53, 60], only a few have thus far withstood some rigor and repeatability, as shown in Figure 5. We will not attempt a complete review of these additional factors here. However, we will outline their potential roles and give an overview of how they interact with the emergent validated trust model.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 5. The emergent trust model in relation to significant external factors.

Continuing to follow the three-layer schema of Hoff and Bashir [60], these additional factors may be divided into three main categories: expanded dispositional trust factors or antecedents, external situational trust factors, and external learned trust factors. Externality is used here to indicate that these factors are not part of the internal trust model, and are directly contingent on the environment and embodiment of the agents in that environment.

9.2.1 Dispositional Antecedents. Dispositional antecedents of trust expand to include those elements outside of the individual’s control, such as their age, culture, and personality. These shape more direct trust-related factors such as the willingness to take risks [29] and one’s faith in people [182] and institutions [37]. Culture, gender, and personality traits, specifically conscientiousness [2], also mediate understandings of group membership [168], group expectations [75], and group cohesiveness[2]. From there, group membership serves to form prior expectations of Familiarity, Situation Normality, and Emotional Response, which influence the Shared Mental Model [159]. Wagner exploited these expectations to extract anticipated rewards, goals, and capability beliefs of virtual agents [168]. Moreover, age and gender seem to guide expectations and cause biases with regard to in-group hierarchies [120], which have a direct impact on robot form. These expanded dispositional factors are discussed in detail in [60], with the role of personality getting a more complete and up-to-date treatment in [2].

9.2.2 Robot Form: An External Situational Factor. Robot form has been a particular area of interest lately, especially its role in mediating trust calibration. Anthropomorphic designs help to combat initial over-trust and boost trust resilience [27, 28, 175], though being ‘too human’ can decrease perceived trustworthiness [54]. These results are aligned with the Perfect Automation Schema, which holds that humans generally think machines to be less biased, fairer, and thus more just [85, 107, 155]. Anthropomorphism primarily affects Situation Normality and Emotional Response, though its effect is confounded through interactions with age, culture, gender, personality, group membership, and educational background, as mentioned above [34]. It should not be forgotten that form is the critical means by which the human assesses and monitors the trustee. Further resources on form and more generally interface design for trust can be found in [149, 169, 172, 178].

9.2.3 External Learned Trust Factors. The three primary factors that affect learned trust are cognitive load, perceived risk, and monitoring. Intent to Use increases with risk [181] and cognitive workload [29]. Perceived risk is a subjective perception of the potential outcome to the trustor given the environment and goal involved and its tolerance is shaped by the trustor’s willingness to risk or their aversion to it [29]. Training and expertise (i.e., a Shared Mental Model based on Familiarity) can help one better calibrate the actual risk involved, as well as how much risk one is able and willing to tolerate. One might think improving a system’s capabilities or accuracy would reduce cognitive load, but this is not the case [22, 25, 170]. Instead, what matters most is the quality of the information provided as feedback during monitoring [22, 59].

Monitoring is the lynch-pin of the external factors for learned trust because it mediates the quality of the feedback loop that allows learning to occur. Monitoring supports updating estimates of goals and their status, risk, current capabilities, loyalties, and rule-following. To do so effectively, monitoring must include data [111], behavior [180], and explainability [1]. As tasks get harder to monitor, frustration and effort increase [59], cognitive load increases, self-confidence decreases, and the user is coerced into trusting the system [148]. Likewise with risk; as the risk associated with the entrusted goal(s) increases, the greater the need for some combination of monitoring, self-confidence, and trust in the system to compensate. While workload is almost always assessed by the NASA TLX [52], assessing risk and ability to monitor (e.g. explainability) is still in its early stages (see [157] and [109], respectively).

The external antecedents and factors that influence trust are by no means exhaustive. However, we feel that the ones described above present the next frontier for validation and testing beyond the internal emergent validated trust model. The model we have presented, therefore, is meant to serve as a foundation for integrating past research into the converging language of trust in technology and automation, while directing future research to attend to the myriad interplays of external factors with trust.

9.2.4 Missing Internal Trust Factors. While we have attempted to create broad categories to describe the results of the emergent validated trust model, there are nuances and differences within factors that we have not fully explored, which are left for future work.

As we have already discussed, there does seem to be a general and detectable distinction between the expectations and confidence in those expectations; this is best seen by the dichotomy in many Capability-based Trust measures, where competence/performance/capability are often found to be distinct from reliability/predictability. While less clear, a similar distinction may be evident within Structural Trust, between the sub-factors of ethical and sincere [90]. There are also some important distinctions expected within Structural Trust as to whether it’s internally or externally motivated [31, 131].

The Situational trust factors have also not been tested together for validity and reliability, and their correlational, and potentially causal, structure is still unknown. It may be that Familiarity and Situation Normality are sub-sets of one another. It is interesting to note how much they co-vary with Emotional Response, speaking to our intuitive understanding that how much comfort or liking we have is dependent on how familiar or normal an agent or interaction appears to be. Emotional Response may be too broad as a single category, but it at least seems that the factors of emotional attachment, liking, enjoyment, warmth, and engagement may be distinct but overlapping in the roles they play in trust development.

Perceived Usefulness has also proven to be a complex category, but mostly due to its textual ambiguity. Many take it descriptively—how useful something is—in the vein of Capability-based Trust. However, some authors have used the term prescriptively, as in how useful something has the potential to be.

One can see from the extended general model that Perceived Risk is accounted for but not potential gains or rewards. The need to account for value-added benefit has explicitly been called out in UTUAT critiques [144] but has received little to no attention in the robotics or automation world in this explicit survey domain. Alternative game theory-based approaches using interdependence theory have begun to shed light on the role of relative expected gains [131].

9.2.5 Distrust. This model does not explicitly deal with distrust. The larger philosophical and cognitive debate over the nature of distrust and its relationship with trust is still ongoing [30, 55]. Ever since Lewicki, McAllister, and Bies [80] posited that trust and distrust were not opposites and should not be measured on the same scale, their relationship with one another has become blurred. Lee and See [78] essentially divorced distrust from the trust calibration conversation, as it was neither over- nor under-trust. The opposite of trust can better be categorized as a combination of distrust and uncertainty. But distrust in the trust literature is often confined very narrowly in the sense of negative Affective Trust (malevolence) or suspicion of such (the negative valence confidence sub-factor of Affective Trust). McKnight and Chervany [100] and Dimoka [30] have given strong descriptions of models that test distrust from a triadic perspective (structural, capability, and affective). An interesting inversion was attempted by [102] where they tested a positively framed trust survey against an equivalent negatively framed one. While insufficient reliability and insufficient validity measures were published on the ‘Negative’ survey, they demonstrated that the negatively valenced survey actually may be more sensitive and have higher explained variance. Therefore, this is less a question of the underlying model, as much as a challenge of framing.

## 10 Designing for Trust and Its Measurement

This work presents three opportunities for advancing trust research. The first is that it provides practical guidance toward picking an appropriate trust survey instrument. The second is that it outlines which factors and antecedents are well-established and which require further research. Finally, by identifying the established factors and antecedents, we can now better understand how to design for trust, and how those interventions and choices affect how trust is thought of.

## 10.1 Picking An Instrument

When picking a trust survey instrument, we must acknowledge that short, one- or two-factor surveys are often appropriate. If too many questions or surveys are to be administered, survey fatigue is a concern. Furthermore, if the task is one where lengthy interruptions cannot be afforded, or the goal is to collect frequent measurements of trust, then shorter trust surveys may be more suitable.

However, if human-automation trust is the main subject under study and its internal structure and dynamics are of interest, then a longer multi-factor survey may be more appropriate. Given its length, this type of survey is best administered before and after the interaction of interest. As mentioned above, the upper-level factors such as Faith in Technology, Familiarity, and Situational Normality will matter more earlier on, especially at the stage of initial acceptance [32, 106] or exposure. It may not be worth measuring these if the interval of test administration is greater than 6 weeks [152]. However, over that period, one could watch how these effects decrease as the effect of factors within Learned Trust increase. Either way, multi-factorial instruments are recommended for longitudinal studies [73]. For similar reasons, differences may arise if one is gauging system trust by new users instead of experts [106].

Whether single or multi-factor instruments are used, the instrument chosen must be adequately tested for reliability and validity. As shown above, several good options covering multiple types of trust construct exist that meet these criteria, and thus the tolerance for ad hoc measures of trust should come to an end. As discussed above (Section 3.1.1), Cronbach’s alpha is generally not a sufficient measure of reliability alone [39]. Reliability should include McDonald’s 𝜔 and the inter-item correlation, if not other methods such as test-retest reliability. Validity should include loadings and communalities for each item on each factor, with at least 4 item loadings of > 0.45 per factor. If a CFA is reported, then $\chi ^ { 2 }$ , the RMSEA, SRMR, and at least two fit indices such as the CFI and TLI, are highly recommended. If using CFI and TLI, they should minimally be $> 0 . 9$ though more recent recommendations range from 0.95 to 0.97. RMSEA and SRMR should at least be below 0.1, though many prefer less than 0.06. However, we also advise against strict cutoffs. Beyond these, the Normality, collinearity, sample size, and sampling adequacy should all be considered. These thresholds and further details on assessing survey quality can be found in [11, 173].

Furthermore, the coverage of factors and antecedents should be considered. Note that of the 15 survey instruments in the meta-analysis, only two had 8 of the 10 identified internal factors, while the average survey covered an average of 5.8 factors. However, if deciding between a survey with more factors or higher reliability and validity, the second should take priority.

## 10.2 Factors for Further Development

While we have established several central factors herein, multiple proposed external factors still exist to substantiate. Given the unclear connection between distrust and factors of trust, separate questions testing the relationship between distrust, uncertainty, and self-confidence are also warranted. Furthermore, the strength and direction of relationships between the 10 internal factors still leave much to be desired. Many relationships remain untested, especially for moderating effects between factors. Of those tested, the majority have only one to two sources, with only nine having three or more. Even among those nine, the bulk face challenges with heterogeneity and outliers. Further analysis, testing, and validation are necessary to gather evidence on these relations.

## 10.3 Guidance for Trustworthy Design

Finally, the identified emergent trust structure yields several lessons when considering how to design for trust. Designers should consider making systems that are easy to use, comfortable, and likable (Emotional Response) using platforms, concepts, and UX from previous iterations or common design conventions in order to increase Situational Normality. Training breeds Familiarity, and that time should be used to also set expectations (initial Shared Mental Model) around how the system achieves its goals (Structural Trust) and its performance quality (Capabilitybased Trust). During training, or even in less formal contexts, organizations should work to build the technologies reputation and have it be recommended. Of course, these strategies should not be used to create over-trust but to calibrate trust appropriately. Misplaced trust can be just as detrimental, especially to trust repair and continued usage [78]. It is also important to remember that the situational trust antecedents are most critical for initial technology acceptance and less so later. Thus, for systems intended for long-term use, more investment should be spent on shaping expectations of the Shared Mental Model, such as having operators do field testing and building expertise. Systems must achieve accuracies of at least 70%–90% to maintain Capability-based trust [78] and avoid easy mistakes, especially misses, which are much more detrimental to trust than false alarms [88]. Systems should also communicate goal recognition and adoption so that users can build Affective trust.

In terms of external factors, transparency, and explainability support monitoring, which can, in turn, strengthen the Shared Mental Model. It should be recognized that high cognitive workload can cause more trust to be placed in the system than is warranted or even consciously intended. Lastly, remember that robot design, such as anthropomorphism, can have both positive and negative effects on group membership, Emotional Response, and even Structural Trust.

## 11 Future Work and Conclusion

This work has described the current state of measuring trust between humans and various technology categories. It has assessed the types of metrics used, especially in terms of reliability, validation, and factor terminology. The latter allowed us to identify ten major trust factors, and the accompanying meta-analysis helped us discern the general structure. We also discussed how trust should be measured going forward, what areas of the model need further examination, and potential avenues to explore—from external trust factors and internal nuances to how trust beliefs become decisions. By evaluating and integrating the results of these previous survey instruments and constructs, the model presented in this work provides a robust foundation for the future of human-machine trust research.
